body:
India's economic system before 1991

After Independence, India adopted a mixed economy, in which public enterprises and private businesses operated together. The government used economic planning to promote industrialisation, agricultural development, infrastructure and self-reliance.

Public enterprises were established in important industries, while private businesses operated under several regulations. Industrial licensing required government permission for many manufacturing activities. High import duties and restrictions on imports protected domestic producers from foreign competition.

This approach is associated with import substitution: producing goods within the country instead of depending heavily on imports. It helped India establish an industrial base and develop domestic production capabilities. However, extensive controls could also limit competition, discourage technological improvements and delay industrial expansion.

Import substitution means encouraging domestic production to replace imports. Export promotion means encouraging domestic producers to sell their goods and services in foreign markets. These are different economic strategies, although a country can pursue both.

Why did India face an economic crisis in 1991?

India faced a severe balance of payments crisis in 1990–1991. The balance of payments records economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world. International payments require foreign exchange, such as US dollars.

Several problems developed together:

  • Large fiscal deficits: Government expenditure substantially exceeded its receipts excluding borrowings, creating a need for borrowing.
  • High external payment requirements: Imports and other foreign payment obligations exceeded the foreign exchange that India could readily obtain.
  • Rising petroleum prices: The 1990 Gulf crisis increased the cost of importing oil.
  • Weakening external financing: International lenders became less willing to provide finance, while external economic disturbances affected trade and remittances.
  • Falling foreign currency assets: India's readily available foreign currency became insufficient to comfortably meet essential international payments.

The Reserve Bank of India's historical account records that India's foreign currency assets fell to approximately US$975 million on 12 July 1991, equivalent to barely a week's imports at that time. This is a historical figure for a specific date, not a statement about India's present foreign exchange reserves.

India faced a serious risk of being unable to meet its external payment obligations. The government obtained external financial assistance and introduced measures to restore economic stability.

Stabilisation and structural reforms

The response involved 2 related but different approaches.

AspectStabilisation measuresStructural reforms
Main purposeControl immediate economic instabilityImprove long-term efficiency and competitiveness
Problems addressedForeign exchange shortages, inflation and fiscal imbalanceExcessive controls, limited competition and barriers to investment
ExamplesExternal financial assistance, import restraint and exchange-rate adjustmentIndustrial delicensing, trade liberalisation and changes in public enterprise policy

Stabilisation deals with an immediate crisis. Structural reform changes the way the economy operates over a longer period. India pursued both approaches in 1991.

Important developments in the reform process

  • 1 and 3 July 1991: The rupee was devalued in 2 stages, with a cumulative downward adjustment of approximately 18% against the US dollar.
  • 24 July 1991: The New Industrial Policy introduced major changes in industrial licensing, private-sector participation and foreign investment.
  • March 1992: India introduced the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System, a transitional dual exchange-rate arrangement.
  • March 1993: The dual exchange-rate system was replaced by a unified market-determined exchange-rate system.

Devaluation is an official downward adjustment in a currency's value under a controlled exchange-rate system. Depreciation refers to a fall in a currency's market value. Both can make imported goods more expensive in domestic currency, while potentially improving the price competitiveness of exports.

The 1991 reforms marked a major change in India's development strategy. They did not end government planning, public enterprises or economic regulation. Instead, they progressively increased the role of markets, competition, private investment and international trade.

Prelims focus

  • India faced a balance of payments crisis in 1990–1991.
  • The rupee was devalued on 1 and 3 July 1991.
  • The New Industrial Policy was announced on 24 July 1991.
  • LERMS was introduced in March 1992; the unified market-determined exchange-rate system followed in March 1993.
  • Trap: The 1991 crisis involved foreign exchange and external payments; it was not simply a shortage of Indian currency.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 3, 'Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal', pp. 39–42; Reserve Bank of India, Reports, 26 June 2000, ch. 1, discussion of the 1991 external payments crisis; Reserve Bank of India, Chronology of Events, 'Crisis and Reforms: 1991 to 2000' (consulted 23 November 2026); Government of India, Economic Survey 1991–92, section 'Industrial Policy Reforms'.]

title: The 1991 Economic Crisis and the Beginning of Economic Reforms

body:
The 3 central concepts

The economic reforms introduced in 1991 are commonly described using the terms liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, often abbreviated as LPG. These concepts are related, but they do not mean the same thing.

ConceptMeaningBasic example
LiberalisationReducing unnecessary restrictions on economic activityRemoving compulsory industrial licences for many industries
PrivatisationIncreasing private ownership or management of economic enterprisesTransferring government ownership or control of an enterprise to private investors
GlobalisationIncreasing integration of national economies with the world economyIndian businesses participating in international production and trade networks

Liberalisation: reducing restrictions

Before 1991, many industries required government permission to establish factories, expand production or undertake other significant activities. The New Industrial Policy substantially reduced industrial licensing and opened additional areas to private participation.

At the time of the July 1991 policy announcement, compulsory licensing was retained for 18 specified industries involving strategic, environmental or other considerations. The list was subsequently reduced through later policy changes. Therefore, the number 18 describes the original 1991 policy position, not a permanent licensing requirement.

Liberalisation also included changes in several other areas:

  • Trade policy: Reducing import licensing, quantitative restrictions and customs duties over time.
  • Investment policy: Permitting greater foreign investment in specified activities and simplifying approval procedures.
  • Financial sector: Increasing competition, allowing new private banks and introducing prudential reforms while retaining regulatory supervision.
  • Taxation: Simplifying procedures and restructuring tax rates to encourage compliance and economic activity.
  • Foreign exchange: Moving progressively towards a market-determined exchange-rate system.

A tariff is a tax on imported goods. A quantitative restriction directly limits the quantity or value of goods that may be imported. Reducing a tariff makes imports less costly; removing a quota permits a larger quantity to enter, subject to other applicable laws.

Liberalisation does not mean that businesses operate without regulation. Banking supervision, environmental protection, product safety and competition law can continue in a liberalised economy.

Privatisation and disinvestment

Privatisation generally refers to transferring government ownership or management to the private sector. Disinvestment means selling part or all of the government's equity in an enterprise.

Disinvestment does not necessarily result in privatisation. If the government sells a minority shareholding but retains control, the enterprise can remain government-controlled. Privatisation normally involves a transfer of control or ownership to private interests.

Governments may also grant public enterprises greater managerial autonomy without selling them. This is neither automatically privatisation nor disinvestment.

Globalisation and international economic integration

Globalisation links countries through trade, investment, technology, services and production. A multinational corporation may obtain materials from one country, manufacture components in another, assemble the product elsewhere and sell it internationally.

The development of container transport, telecommunications and information technology made such international connections easier. Trade liberalisation reduced some policy barriers to the movement of goods and services.

Foreign investment and foreign trade are different

Foreign direct investment (FDI) involves an investor obtaining a lasting interest and significant influence in an enterprise located in another economy. For example, a foreign company establishing a manufacturing subsidiary in Gujarat represents direct investment.

Foreign portfolio investment generally involves investment in financial assets, such as shares or bonds, without obtaining the same lasting managerial influence.

Foreign trade involves buying or selling goods and services across national borders. Importing machinery does not, by itself, mean that the foreign machinery producer has made direct investment in India.

World Trade Organization

The World Trade Organization (WTO) came into existence in 1995 as the successor to the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade framework. It provides a system of agreed rules for international trade and a mechanism for resolving trade disputes between members.

The WTO does not require every country to remove every trade restriction. Members retain policy powers subject to their agreed obligations, exceptions and applicable rules.

Prelims focus

  • Liberalisation reduces restrictions on economic activity.
  • Privatisation concerns private ownership or management; disinvestment concerns the sale of government equity.
  • The New Industrial Policy was announced in July 1991.
  • The WTO was established in 1995.
  • Trap: Every instance of disinvestment does not transfer government control to the private sector.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 3, pp. 41–47; NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, ch. 4, 'Globalisation and the Indian Economy', pp. 55–69; Government of India, Economic Survey 1991–92, section 'Industrial Policy Reforms', p. 12 (consulted 23 November 2026).]

title: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: Meaning and Major Policy Changes

body:
How economic integration changed production

After the 1991 reforms, Indian producers faced greater opportunities to sell internationally and greater competition from imported goods. Foreign investment and the movement of technology connected many Indian businesses with international production networks.

Globalisation can increase the range of goods available to consumers. Competition may encourage producers to improve quality, reduce costs and introduce new technology. However, businesses unable to compete with cheaper imports or larger firms may lose sales or employment.

Examples of internationally connected activities

  • Information technology and business services: Indian firms provide software, customer support, accounting and other services to clients abroad.
  • Manufacturing: Indian factories may import machinery or components and sell finished products in domestic and foreign markets.
  • Textiles and garments: Producers may receive orders from international buyers, subject to requirements concerning quality, delivery and price.
  • Gujarat's diamond industry: Rough diamonds can be imported, cut and polished in Surat, and then exported. The value added through processing is different from the total value of the imported rough stones or exported polished stones.
  • Gujarat's petroleum industry: Refineries may process imported crude oil and supply petroleum products to domestic and international markets.

These examples demonstrate that globalisation involves the organisation of production as well as international buying and selling.

Economic growth and economic development

Economic growth means an increase in an economy's production of goods and services, usually measured through real GDP or real GSDP. Economic development is broader: it includes improvements in income, employment opportunities, health, education and living conditions.

At the national level, gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of final goods and services produced within India during a specified period. At the state level, gross state domestic product (GSDP) performs a similar function for economic activity within the state.

Real growth adjusts for price changes. An increase in nominal GDP caused only by rising prices does not mean that the economy has produced more goods and services.

Per capita income divides aggregate income by population. It gives an average, but it does not reveal whether income is distributed equally among people.

Changes in the relative importance of economic sectors

SectorMain activitiesExamples
PrimaryUsing or extracting natural resourcesFarming, animal husbandry, fishing
SecondaryManufacturing and constructionTextiles, refining, construction
TertiaryProviding servicesTransport, banking, trade, IT services

The expansion of services became an important feature of India's post-reform economy. Financial services, telecommunications, transport and information technology created new forms of economic activity.

However, the contribution of a sector to output and its contribution to employment are not necessarily proportional. Agriculture may account for a relatively smaller share of economic output while continuing to support a large number of livelihoods.

Why growth does not automatically remove inequality

Economic growth can increase incomes and public revenue, but its benefits depend on the distribution of opportunities and resources.

  • Differences in skills: Workers with education and specialised skills may benefit more from growing technology-intensive industries.
  • Differences in assets: Owners of land, businesses or capital may gain more from expanding markets than workers with few assets.
  • Differences between regions: Places with roads, reliable electricity, ports and trained workers may attract more investment.
  • Differences in employment conditions: Formal jobs may provide more stable wages and social protection than informal or casual work.
  • Exposure to competition: Small farmers and manufacturers may face unstable prices or competition from larger domestic and foreign producers.

Employment-intensive growth creates substantial work opportunities as production expands. Where output rises through highly productive machinery or technology without a similar increase in employment, growth may not create enough jobs for all workers seeking them.

There is also a difference between open unemployment, where a person seeking work cannot find employment, and disguised unemployment, where more people work in an activity than are needed to produce its existing output. Disguised unemployment is often illustrated through small agricultural holdings.

Social change associated with economic transformation

Industrialisation and the growth of services can encourage migration to towns and cities, changes in occupations, greater participation in education and new opportunities for women. Access to technology and communication can also influence consumption patterns and cultural practices.

These changes are not uniform. Migration can bring higher earnings and more employment choices, but it can also create housing shortages, insecure work and pressure on public services.

Gujarat also has an important example of collective organisation among informal workers. The Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA) was founded in Ahmedabad in 1972 by Ela Bhatt. It organises self-employed women and other women working in the informal economy. Its establishment predates the 1991 reforms, showing that efforts to improve economic participation and working conditions have a longer history.

Prelims focus

  • GDP measures economic output; economic development also concerns people's living conditions.
  • GSDP measures economic production within a state.
  • Primary, secondary and tertiary activities are distinguished by the nature of production.
  • Surat is associated with diamond cutting, polishing and textiles.
  • SEWA was founded in Ahmedabad in 1972 by Ela Bhatt.
  • Trap: A higher share of GDP does not necessarily mean a higher share of employment.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, ch. 3, pp. 45–53; NCERT, Understanding Economic Development, Class 10, chs. 1, 2 and 4, 'Development', 'Sectors of the Indian Economy' and 'Globalisation and the Indian Economy'; NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, ch. 9, 'Globalisation'; Self-Employed Women's Association, Annual Report 2022, p. 3, organisational history (consulted 23 November 2026).]
